solutions.check: 32 entries; each light the paper's grid did not give solved here from its clue's wordplay (an anagram or hidden word, the one listed word fitting every crossing) and its definition (WordNet), as the answer another puzzle gave the same clue, or as the one past answer its crossings left that the printed letters allow, agrees with the 31 answers the paper printed

clue.text: Trusted he had got round the work

indicators.note: got round says the contraction of he had is wrapped about the next piece

parts.note: he had contracts to he'd
OP, short for opus, is a work of music

explanation.surface: Someone believed a man had managed to get round a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got round' puts OP inside HE'D, the contraction of 'he had'.
explanation.definitionFit: To have trusted that something would happen is to have wished and expected it.

clue.text: Records of one man's political adherents

parts.note: belonging to one man is his
Tories are adherents of the Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A list of the supporters of a single party politician.
explanation.walkthrough: TORIES are members of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Histories are chronicles, written accounts of past events.

explanation.surface: Someone paints the garden fences white.
explanation.definitionFit: To pale is to go white or lose colour; pales are also the pointed stakes of a fence, as in a paling.

parts.note: a tedious old Scotsman; the name is that of Sir Walter Scott's pedantic antiquary to whom he addressed prefaces, now a word for any dull scholar

explanation.walkthrough: Dr Jonas Dryasdust is the fictional antiquary of Sir Walter Scott's prefaces, so 'Scottish' points to Scott, not to Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A dull pedantic scholar is called by the name of Scott's tedious antiquarian character.

parts.note: brief means short
a wave of the hand is a greeting

explanation.surface: A breezy, quick hello.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Airy' is not light-hearted here: it means on the air, broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: Short-wave radio is sent over the air, so it belongs to the airwaves.

explanation.surface: Someone enjoyed themselves and made no secret of it.
explanation.definitionFit: To sport is to play or frolic, and to sport something is to wear or display it proudly.

clue.text: After one month Mark Antony had a way with her

definitions.text: After one month Mark Antony had a way with her

parts.note: Oct is the short form of October
via is Latin for road or way

explanation.surface: After a month's courtship the Roman general charmed a lady.
explanation.walkthrough: VIA is Latin for 'way', apt for a Roman wife; the whole clue also describes her, the woman Mark Antony married.
explanation.definitionFit: Octavia, sister of Octavian, was the Roman general's wife before Cleopatra drew him away.

clue.text: He instructs that in France you go to the right

parts.note: tu is the French familiar word for you
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A teacher explains that in France one keeps to the right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in France' makes the next word French: 'you' is TU.
explanation.definitionFit: A tutor is a private teacher, one who instructs pupils.

clue.text: Where to go the pace and swagger in Westmorland

parts.note: to go at an easy walking pace is to amble
side is old slang for swagger or putting on airs

explanation.surface: Where in the Lake District to stroll and show off.
explanation.walkthrough: SIDE, meaning conceit or pretentious airs, is dated British slang. Westmorland was an English county in the Lake District, now part of Cumbria; 'Where' opens the clue and points to a place there.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambleside is a town at the head of Windermere, in the former county.

clue.text: Monsieur in blue coming up to take tests

indicators.note: in a down clue coming up means the letters read from bottom to top
in says the abbreviation for Monsieur goes inside the colour

parts.note: saxe is a light greyish blue

explanation.surface: A Frenchman in a sad mood arrives to sit his examinations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts M inside SAXE, making SMAXE; 'coming up' turns it to read EXAMS. 'blue' looks like sadness but is the colour saxe.
explanation.definitionFit: Exams are examinations, formal tests of knowledge.

clue.text: Whence Miss Lunn emerges with the wine

parts.note: Sally Lunn is the girl's name given to a teacake
port is a fortified wine

explanation.surface: From where a lady comes out carrying the wine.
explanation.walkthrough: A sally is a sortie from a fortress, so 'emerges' hints at the sense of the whole. Sally Lunn is a sweet bun from Bath, named after a supposed baker.
explanation.definitionFit: A sally port is a gate in a fortification through which troops make a sortie, the place they come out from.

clue.text: To thee an ancient pipe, O Roman

parts.note: tibi is Latin for to thee, the 'O Roman' telling the solver to use Latin

explanation.surface: A Roman offers someone an old flute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'O Roman' addresses a Roman, which tells the solver to put 'To thee' into Latin, TIBI.
explanation.definitionFit: The tibia was the reed flute of ancient Rome, named after the shin bone it was first made from.

parts.note: Omar Khayyam's poem has a loaf, a jug of wine and a companion in the wilderness, so the picnic spot is a fertile place in a desert

explanation.walkthrough: In FitzGerald's Rubaiyat, Omar wants bread, wine and 'thou beside me singing in the Wilderness': a green spot in the desert suits.
explanation.definitionFit: An oasis is a watered, fertile place in a desert, the kind of wilderness picnic the poem describes.

parts.note: keepers of inns are an old term for them, and the Lord's cricket ground lends its name to a charity society

explanation.walkthrough: The Lord's Taverners is a British cricket charity named after the tavern at Lord's, London's famous cricket ground; 'lordly' points there.
explanation.definitionFit: Taverners are keepers of taverns, and the Lord's Taverners are a celebrated cricketing club.

parts.note: a command to seize stray animals and shut them in an enclosure

explanation.walkthrough: Stray animals are shut in a pound, so the word that means 'seize' also means put the beasts in their pen.
explanation.definitionFit: To impound is to confiscate, and literally to shut stray livestock in a pound.

clue.text: Arabian speciality not unknown in ancient Scotland

definitions.text: Arabian speciality not unknown in ancient Scotland

parts.words: Arabian speciality not unknown in ancient Scotland
parts.note: scents of Arabia are what Lady Macbeth says will not sweeten her hand in Shakespeare's Scottish play

explanation.walkthrough: Lady Macbeth says 'All the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand', so Arabian scents were known in Macbeth's ancient Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Perfumery means perfumes collectively, the scents the play links to Arabia.

clue.text: Vespucci, it seems, missed a round!

indicators.note: it seems signals that the name only sounds like the phrase

parts.note: the fairground ride a merry-go-round, missing its word round, leaves a merry-go

explanation.surface: An explorer apparently skipped a lap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missed a round' means take 'round' off 'a merry-go-round', leaving 'a merry-go'; 'it seems' says that phrase sounds like the explorer's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Amerigo Vespucci was the Florentine navigator whose first name gave America its name.

parts.note: a sub-editor cuts copy, and an officer bound up with duty on goods collects taxes

explanation.walkthrough: To excise is to cut out, a sub-editor's job; an exciseman was the old British official who collected excise duty.
explanation.definitionFit: An exciseman is a tax officer who collects excise, a duty charged on goods.

annotationWithheld.why: Read novel when oppressed (9): OVERLADEN is an anagram of READ + NOVEL, but 'novel' would have to be both fodder and the anagram indicator

indicators.note: from says the beings are made out of the letters of the word priests

explanation.surface: Clergymen arriving from fairyland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' tells the solver to rearrange PRIESTS; the beings so made belong to Elfland.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprites are elves and fairies, the inhabitants of a fairyland.

parts.note: George Meredith wrote a comic fantasy about the shaving of a hairy character

explanation.walkthrough: George Meredith's novel 'The Shaving of Shagpat' (1856) tells of a barber who shaves a clothier.
explanation.definitionFit: Shagpat is the title character whose shaving gives Meredith's novel its plot.

clue.text: Weapon that might be used to cheat me

indicators.note: might be used to suggests the letters of cheat me can be reworked to make the weapon

explanation.surface: A blade that someone could employ to swindle me.
explanation.definitionFit: A machete is a broad heavy knife, a blade used as a tool and as an arm.

clue.text: Lourenço is thus disguised at the fancy dress ball

definitions.text: Lourenço is thus disguised at the fancy dress ball

indicators.note: disguised says the surname is given a different look, its letters rearranged

parts.note: Lourenço Marques was the Mozambican port named after a Portuguese explorer, so the name brings its surname

explanation.surface: A man called Lourenço wears a costume at a masked ball.
explanation.walkthrough: Lourenço Marques (now Maputo) was the capital of Portuguese Mozambique; 'Lourenço' calls up MARQUES, which 'disguised' rearranges into a reveller at a masked ball.
explanation.definitionFit: A masquer is a person taking part in a masquerade, wearing a mask or costume.

parts.note: Old Father Time is pictured holding a scythe and a glass running with sand; also a figure narrow at the waist

explanation.walkthrough: Father Time carries a sand-glass, and an hourglass figure is a woman's shape with a narrow waist, so 'figure' works both ways.
explanation.definitionFit: An hourglass is the sand timer that Father Time carries.

parts.note: Aries is the Ram of the zodiac, and a tup is a ram

explanation.surface: A man makes the Ram restless.
explanation.walkthrough: TUP is a northern British word for a ram.
explanation.definitionFit: Het up is a colloquial phrase for worked up or excited.

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: to drag is to pull

explanation.surface: Someone stops beside a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns DRAG to GARD.
explanation.definitionFit: Garda is the largest lake in Italy.

clue.text: The lady will in short prove a hard case

parts.note: a lady is she
will is shortened to 'll in a contraction

explanation.surface: A woman will turn out to be a tough nut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in short' marks a contraction: 'The lady will' becomes SHE'LL.
explanation.definitionFit: A shell is a hard outer covering, a hard case.

parts.note: a way in, and also each item written in the ledger by a careful clerk

explanation.walkthrough: The word means a way in, and also an item written in accounts, as in double-entry bookkeeping.
explanation.definitionFit: An entry is an entrance or gateway, and a record made in a ledger.

clue.text: Attribution of ownership among the Irish

indicators.note: among says the letters sit within the words the Irish

explanation.surface: The Irish word that says what belongs to whom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' marks letters sitting inside 'the Irish'.
explanation.definitionFit: The possessive word belonging to 'they' states that something is theirs to own.

clue.text: Sank deep when prize job was apportioned

parts.note: a plum is a choice, much-coveted job
meted, as in meted out, means apportioned

explanation.surface: Someone's spirits fell when the best post was handed out.
explanation.definitionFit: To have plummeted is to have fallen steeply, dropped like a weight.

annotationWithheld.why: Mary's a pet, generally speaking (9): PAYMASTER is an anagram of MARYS A PET with 'generally' pointing to Paymaster-General, but there is no anagram indicator and no definition separate from that pun

parts.note: nay means no
yon is an old word for yonder

explanation.surface: Someone points, saying no, Calvin was born over there.
explanation.definitionFit: Noyon is the French town in Picardy where the reformer John Calvin was born.
